scenes.headline: How speculative decoding drafts, verifies, and sometimes loses
scenes.sub: Five drafting methods, nine models, in vLLM on AMD GPUs.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Poppy! Speculative decoding lets a small drafter guess ahead while the big model checks its work. Here's how that works, and when it doesn't pay.

scenes.text: A cheap drafter guesses tokens; the big model checks them all in one pass.
scenes.say: The idea: a cheap drafter proposes several tokens, and the big model verifies all of them in a single pass, keeping the part it agrees with.

steps.say: The drafter reads the context and proposes four tokens: sunny, and, warm, outside.
The target checks all four in one pass, left to right. Sunny and and survive. Warm is rejected, and everything after it is thrown away.
The target supplies its own token, clear. Three tokens committed for one pass of the big model.

left.title: Sequential drafters
items: Pays only for what it proposes
left.say: Sequential drafters, like MTP and EAGLE-3, guess one token at a time. They pay only for what they propose, so in the tests, longer proposals never gave gains back.

right.title: Parallel drafters
items: DFlash: a whole block at once
right.say: DFlash drafts a whole block in one pass, and pays to verify all of it. On one model it peaked near seven tokens, then declined.

scenes.title: EAGLE-3 speed ratio, Qwen3-8B on MATH500
scenes.note: throughput against not speculating at all
scenes.say: And sometimes it loses. EAGLE-3 on Qwen3-8B, on math, is slower than not speculating at every length tested. The baseline is already too fast.

scenes.text: A drafting method's speedup is a function of model, workload and proposal length, not one number.
scenes.say: So a drafting method's speedup is a function of the model, the workload and the proposal length. It is not one number.
To recap: draft cheap, verify in one pass, and measure on your own model and workload.
